first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent this so I read it properly, top to bottom. I liked that it says where things come from and doesn't make things up. "Where a story is only 'often told', we say so." That's honest. And it mentions the legal registry office straight away, which is what I actually worry about.

journey.quote: Each custom is grouped by when it happens, from the week before to the morning after, and each meaning comes from a German heritage body, a German government page or a named editorial source.
journey.reaction: Good. Sensible, sourced, not chatty. I can follow it on the iPad.

journey.quote: Plan where the porcelain will be broken and who supplies the brooms, since the clean-up is part of the custom.
journey.reaction: Practical. I'd be the one worrying about the broken plates and Mum walking near them, so I'm glad someone thought about it.

journey.quote: So plan in that order: secure the Standesamt first, then build the church, garden or castle celebration around it.
journey.reaction: Clear, and exactly what I'd want my daughter to know before anyone pays for a castle.

journey.section: What an Australian couple should check
journey.quote: Notice periods, the full document list, translations and whether the ceremony can be held in English are all set locally, so check with the Standesamt where you plan to marry.
journey.reaction: Fair enough, but this is where I start thinking: who does the checking, and who reads the German forms? The next section half answers it.

journey.section: Getting married in Germany from Australia
journey.quote: This section is general information, not legal advice. Your Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements with the Standesamt in writing before you book.
journey.reaction: That's what I want to hear. In writing, before booking. I'd show that line to my husband.

journey.section: Getting married in Germany from Australia
journey.quote: One person works in your time zone and plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments with you, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: One named person and the fee in writing. That's reassuring. It doesn't say anything about deposits held by German suppliers or contracts in German, though.

journey.quote: At some point after the ceremony, close friends "kidnap" the bride and take her from bar to bar while the groom tries to find them, sometimes leaving him the bill.
journey.reaction: A bit of fun, but I'd quietly hope my daughter skips this one. Not a problem with the article.

journey.quote: A foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof of marriage, but may not work as proof of a name change, and Smartraveller suggests a lawyer to confirm validity.
journey.reaction: Useful. I wouldn't have thought of the name change. That's the sort of thing a parent wants flagged.

unanswered_questions: If a German venue or supplier takes a deposit and then lets us down, who is responsible and is the money protected?
Are contracts with German suppliers translated into English, and are quotes in AUD or euros?
Who do we ring if something goes wrong on the day, given the time difference?
My mother has trouble walking. Does the Wedded Advisor help with accessible venues, transfers and travel insurance for older guests?
Can I speak to someone on the phone before anything is booked?
would_share_with: My husband, with the Standesamt section and the 'in writing' line highlighted
My daughter, to say yes, do the registry office first

cta_reaction.quote: If the paperwork is the part keeping you up at night, speak with a Wedded Advisor.
cta_reaction.why: The paperwork is exactly what keeps me up at night, so it speaks to me. But I'd want a phone number or to know someone will actually ring me back. I'd probably let my daughter enquire and ask to be on the call.

top_3_changes: Near the Wedded Advisor paragraph, add one sentence on how deposits and supplier contracts are handled (who checks them, who is accountable), even if it just says the Advisor reviews them with you.
Say plainly that you can book a phone call, so a parent knows she can talk to a person before anything is paid.
A short line on older or less mobile guests (transfers, accessible venues, travel insurance) would make this feel like it was written for families, not just the couple.

stayed in character as Margaret (funding parent)
no invented brand facts; missing information listed in unanswered_questions
VERIFY markers and HTML comments ignored
business details deferred and no prices treated as standard, not raised as must-fix

open_questions.question: Deposit protection, contract language and accessibility for elderly guests are unanswered. Treat as nice-to-have for a traditions post, or route to CRO for the CTA block?
